title: Your own voice
hook: the Prophet ﷺ liked to hear the Qur'an from others (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tajwid: the stretch, the hum and the stop. Your line was every letter is due its right. Did you catch one held vowel, or let someone finish their sentence? Day two hundred twenty-nine.

A voice played back on a voicemail or in a video can sound thin and strange, not like its owner at all. And after yesterday's rules, it would be easy to think the Qur'an belongs to the professionals, the famous reciters with voices like cellos. But there's a story in Bukhari that turns this upside down. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the one the Qur'an was revealed to, turned to a companion and asked him to recite. The companion was baffled. Recite to you? It was sent down to you. And the Prophet said: I like to hear it from someone else. Today: zayyinu.
screen: `A VOICE PLAYED BACK.` → `RECITE TO YOU?` → `I LIKE TO HEAR IT FROM SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: The companion was Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He began reciting Surah an-Nisa'. He reached the verse that asks how it will be when a witness is brought from every people, and the Prophet himself is brought as witness over them. The Prophet said: enough. Ibn Mas'ud looked up and saw tears running from his eyes. The one who received the words was moved by hearing them in another man's voice. Other reports make the same point from different sides. The Prophet heard Abu Musa al-Ash'ari reciting one night and told him he'd been given a flute, a mizmar, like those of the family of the prophet Dawud, David. And in Abu Dawud's collection the Prophet says: beautify the Qur'an with your voices. Zayyinu, make it lovely. Not your voice made lovely by the Qur'an: the Qur'an made lovely by your voice. Scholars have discussed what that allows and draw the line in different places, but a common thread runs through them: a beautiful, moving voice is praised, as long as the tajwid is kept and the recitation doesn't turn into a performance of songs. Another hadith says he is not of us who doesn't recite the Qur'an with taghanni, a word some read as chanting it melodiously and others as being content with it. Either way, the invitation is plain. The beauty isn't only in the famous voices. It's also in the ordinary voice that's trying.
screen: `IBN MAS'UD RECITES, THE PROPHET WEEPS.` · `ABU MUSA'S FLUTE.` · `ZAYYINU — MAKE IT LOVELY.` · `THE ORDINARY VOICE THAT TRIES.` · then, large: `BEAUTIFY IT WITH YOUR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Find a spot where you can be heard only by yourself. Choose something short: the bismillah, the first line of the Fatiha, or one verse in English if that's what you have. Take a breath. Now say it out loud, once, slowly, at a normal volume. Not a whisper. Let your voice be exactly what it is. Then sit in the quiet after it and notice how it felt to hear it in your own voice rather than someone else's. If you'd like, say it once more, a little slower. The bell holds the time.
Zayyinu, beautify: what the Prophet told people to do to the Qur'an with their own voices, after he himself asked to hear it recited by others.
Your line: beautify it with your voice. Once today, say one line you love out loud, to no one but yourself, and let it be heard in your own voice. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims recite the Qur'an aloud in prayer, in study circles, and at home; many listen to well-known reciters, and teachers encourage students to recite in their own voice with care and feeling rather than imitating a performance.

fork.reveal: he asked exactly that. the Prophet said: I like to hear it from someone else. then he wept at 4:41 (Bukhari).

original.note: Arabic: beautify, make lovely. zayyinu l-Qur'an bi-aswatikum.

trapdoor: what you thought: only trained reciters should recite aloud.
what it means: the Prophet loved to hear the Qur'an from others and told people to beautify it with their own voices.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 5050 (Ibn Mas'ud and 4:41); Bukhari 5048 (Abu Musa's mizmar); Abu Dawud 1468 (zayyinu); taghanni read two ways.
